## More Than Medication: The Pharmacist’s Role in End-of-Life Care


**November is National Hospice and Palliative Care Month, an opportunity to recognize the professionals who help patients and families navigate serious illness and end-of-life care with comfort, dignity and support.**


For patients approaching the end of life, the goals of medication therapy often begin to change. Preventing disease progression years into the future may become less important, while managing pain, shortness of breath, agitation, nausea and other symptoms takes greater priority.


That shift can make medication management both more important and more complex.


Patients may have multiple chronic conditions, significant symptom burden, changing organ function and difficulty swallowing. Medication regimens that were appropriate months or years earlier may no longer provide meaningful benefit. At the same time, new medications may need to be initiated, adjusted or delivered through alternative routes as a patient’s condition changes.


Whether a patient is receiving hospice care at home, in a hospice house or while living in a long-term care or senior living community, pharmacists can provide clinical expertise that helps the care team align medication therapy with the patient’s changing needs and goals.


National palliative care guidance recognizes pharmacists as part of the interdisciplinary team, with responsibilities that can include medication review, symptom management, patient and caregiver education, collaboration and support during transitions of care.1


#### **Managing Symptoms with Comfort in Mind**


Pain is one of the most recognized concerns at the end of life, but it is far from the only one. Dyspnea, nausea and vomiting, delirium or agitation, constipation, secretions and difficulty swallowing can all affect comfort and quality of life.


Pharmacists can help assess medication-related contributors to these symptoms, recommend appropriate therapies, evaluate dosing and routes of administration, monitor for adverse effects and help the care team adjust treatment as the patient’s condition changes. The goal is not simply to treat a symptom, but to continually evaluate whether therapy is providing relief while remaining consistent with the patient’s goals of care.


Sometimes, that requires addressing fears about the medications themselves.


One pharmacist’s encounter with a resident illustrates how much listening can reveal. The resident’s pain was not adequately controlled, but she was afraid to try the medication her physician had recommended.


By sitting with her and talking through her concerns, the pharmacist helped explain the proposed treatment and learned more about her children, her love of crossword puzzles and her life beyond her illness. The conversation offered a fuller understanding of her pain and concerns. The pharmacist identified opportunities to adjust her medication therapy and shared those insights with the physician, nursing leadership and hospice team to support her comfort.


It was a clinical intervention, but also a reminder that effective end-of-life care begins with listening to the person receiving it.


#### **Solving Medication Challenges at the Bedside**


Clinical expertise can also help the care team find practical solutions when cost, availability or formulation becomes a barrier to comfort.
[Megan McDowell](https://www.linkedin.com/in/megan-b-mcdowell/) , Pharm.D., Consultant Pharmacist with Guardian Pharmacy of Colorado, encountered this challenge when a hospice patient developed severe oral mucositis that was causing significant pain. The hospice team considered a commercially available compounded mouthwash, but its cost presented a barrier to timely treatment.


After consulting with the hospice physician, McDowell recommended a more cost-effective and personalized alternative. She provided guidance on formulation and administration, allowing the patient to receive treatment promptly while substantially reducing cost.


For hospice organizations, interventions like this can serve two purposes at once: helping improve patient comfort while supporting responsible management of medication spend.


#### **Extending the Interdisciplinary Care Team**


Perhaps the pharmacist’s greatest value in end-of-life care comes from bringing medication expertise into a larger conversation.


Palliative and hospice care are inherently interdisciplinary. Pharmacists work alongside physicians, nurses, hospice clinicians, caregivers and other members of the care team to identify medication-related problems, recommend changes, educate patients and families and help ensure therapies remain aligned with the patient’s goals. The role can be particularly valuable during transitions between hospitals, long-term care communities, hospice houses and home, when medication reconciliation, access and clear handoff communication become especially important.


For patients with dementia, that collaboration may become even more important as disease progression makes it harder for the individual to describe symptoms or participate in decision-making. Palliative care providers have emphasized the importance of helping families establish goals of care before decisions become crisis-driven and of supporting caregivers as needs become more complex.2


For long-term care and hospice pharmacy teams, supporting end-of-life care ultimately means looking beyond the medication list. It means asking what the patient needs now, what may no longer be helping, what is creating unnecessary burden and what can be done to provide greater comfort.


Sometimes that means recommending a different medication or dose. Sometimes it means finding a more accessible formulation, simplifying a regimen or helping a family understand why a medication is changing.


And sometimes it means sitting beside a patient, listening to stories about her children and her crossword puzzles, and working together with the care team to prioritize what matters most to her.


**References**


1. Uritsky T. *While the Credits Roll: The Pharmacist’s Role in End-of-Life Care.* American Pharmacists Association 2026 Annual Meeting & Exposition; Los Angeles, CA; March 27–30, 2026.
2. How palliative care dovetails with the GUIDE dementia care model. *Hospice News.* Published September 5, 2025. Accessed October 21, 2026.
